name: King Saul
charge: Unlawful sacrifice; sparing what was devoted; consulting a medium
summary: A king undone by a pattern of partial obedience. He offered a sacrifice that was not his to offer, spared Agag and the best of the spoil against a direct command, and at the end sought a medium the law condemned.
offense: Saul's fall began with a command displaced by pressure. At Gilgal he saw the people scattering and the Philistines gathering. Samuel had instructed him to wait, but Saul offered the burnt offering and defended himself by naming the circumstances that frightened him (1 Samuel 10:8; 13:8-12). He had not been given authority to change the command because waiting became difficult. The trial exposed whose word governed him when the people grew afraid.
judgment: The kingdom was torn from him and given to another. 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' He died by his own hand on Gilboa the next day, his sons with him.

entries.commentary: Chapter 13 is the beginning of Saul showing his simplicity, the beginning of the proof that he is not fit to be king over Israel. Saul chose three thousand men, two thousand with him in Michmash and mount Bethel and a thousand with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. Jonathan smote the garrison of the Philistines in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it; Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, and Israel was had in abomination with the Philistines. His son popped off the battle, so now it is war time.

The Philistines gathered thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand on the seashore, far deeper than the three thousand Israel had prepared. When the men of Israel saw they were in a strait, they hid themselves in caves, thickets, rocks, high places, and pits; some Hebrews fled over Jordan, and the people that followed Saul followed him trembling. The sons of God, the mighty men of valor, saw the enemy coming and started hiding. As the chosen people, if we really have faith we should be fearless; the Lord had just defeated the Philistines for Israel in chapter 7. To still fear the enemy shows a lack of faith, that you really do not believe in your God. Nehemiah shows the right spirit. In the Persian captivity he had liberty from the king to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and the enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem plotted to scare him off the work. A hired man urged him to hide in the temple because they were coming to slay him, and Nehemiah refused; operating in the spirit of fear is sin according to the scripture.

Samuel had instructed Saul in chapter 10: when you get to Gilgal, tarry seven days, make no moves until I arrive. Saul tarried seven days according to the set time, but Samuel came not at the moment expected, and the people were scattered from him and acting frantic. Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and he offered the burnt offering, and Saul is not the priest; that is Samuel's office. And it came to pass that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. He was barely late, and Saul could not hold his patience. Brothers do the same thing today: leadership said it would be here at ten, it is five past ten, so we cancel the plan and go home. Be humble and tarry like you were instructed; it may run some minutes over, and the Lord may be testing your patience.

Samuel asks, What hast thou done? Saul answers with excuses: the people were scattered from me, thou camest not within the days appointed, the Philistines gathered at Michmash, so I forced myself and offered a burnt offering. This is part of Saul's pattern of behavior; he never wants to hold himself accountable, he always deflects onto whoever else.

Samuel does not entertain the excuses: thou hast done foolishly; thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God. Saul thought he was only bending Samuel's word, but disobeying the instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord. For now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever; but now thy kingdom shall not continue. For that one act of foolishness the Lord withdrew what he would have given: Saul's lineage ruling Israel. The Lord wants to see whether you will perform what he told you to do even when things do not work out how you planned; that is what proves you faithful in temptation and worthy of being exalted. Saul failed that test in the time of his distress. The Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart to be captain over his people. Samuel prophesied this without ever having met the replacement; that man is David, predestined before he is even introduced in the scriptures.

Samuel went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin, and Saul numbered the people present with him, about six hundred men. The Philistines encamped in Michmash, and the spoilers came out of their camp in three companies, toward Ophrah, toward Bethhoron, and toward the border overlooking the valley of Zeboim; three raiding parties sent out to invade Israel.

There was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears. The Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his share, his coulter, his axe, and his mattock, so the Philistines knew exactly how disarmed Israel was; all they had was a file for the tools. This is heavy for today. A people that must depend on its adversary for weaponry cannot deliver itself by arms; talk of going to war means nothing when you have to buy your weapons from the very gun store of the ones you say you will fight. Same picture as the scriptures. So in the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear in the hand of any of the people, but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found; only two men in the army had a blade. In chapter 13 Saul blew the kingdom with his instability in a time of distress. The Most High said, You are not fit; I would have established you, but your replacement is already on the way.

Samuel said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people; now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way when he came up from Egypt. Generations after the wilderness, the Most High still remembers; the generation of Amalekites had returned, and it was time to fulfil what was written. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass. This is a specific instruction: kill all of them, spare none. Note that the Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness; that answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows [Leviticus 19:18](/bible/leviticus/19#v18) applies to the children of thy people.

Saul gathered the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen and ten thousand men of Judah, and laid wait in the valley. Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed. The Most High discriminates righteously: the people who showed Israel kindness were spared out of the judgment.

Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, and utterly destroyed the people with the edge of the sword; but he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive. He halfway fulfilled the order, reasoning like the king might be valuable as a hostage, as if the Lord forgot that detail. But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them; but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly. They killed what looked like it deserved killing, so they could say they did some killing, and kept the healthy, good looking animals, telling themselves surely the Lord could not have meant these.

Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel: It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king, for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. Mark the language: Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counts it as turning back and not performing his commandments at all. For everybody who says, well, I did do this part, understand: whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you. That is what the Most High is showing us in this story. And it grieved Samuel, and he cried unto the Lord all night. Pride had to be in operation for Saul to transgress on that level, and pride is where the throne is lost.

Samuel rose early to meet Saul, and it was told him that Saul came to Carmel and set him up a place, a monument to himself, and is gone down to Gilgal. When your transgression becomes the lesson, be thankful when the correction comes quietly and nobody knows your name; do not take the spirit of bitterness, because you deserved a lot more. Saul greets Samuel first with a cover: Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord. The first thing out of his mouth is a fabrication, knowing full well he transgressed. Samuel answers, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear? If you performed the commandment, why do I hear animals? Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. Verse 9 already told us Saul and the people spared them; now suddenly it is only the people, and for a good reason, a sacrifice, as though the Lord ought to be pleased.

Samuel said, Stay, and I will tell thee what the Lord hath said to me this night. When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel? Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance: when you thought nothing of yourself, with no confidence to be a ruler, the Most High still chose you. And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed; the errand was the vengeance written in [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25). Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

Saul is in denial: Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. Samuel breaks down the rebuke and Saul tells the prophet he is wrong. In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted; then he lays the spoil on the people again: the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.

Samuel makes it plain: Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Do you think the Lord prefers a sacrifice to atone for broken commandments over you simply keeping the commandments? That is a heavy verse.

For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. That is heavy. A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in. This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last; we will read Saul's end in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.

Now the confession finally comes, and it is still not sincere: I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord and thy words; because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. Even in admitting it he deflects: it is the fault of the wicked people you put me over. Then he asks, Pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord; take me back to the regular Saul and Samuel connection, as though a fearful excuse settles it.

Samuel refuses: I will not return with thee; for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. Think it through: Samuel gave Saul the opening at the bleating of the sheep, and Saul would not humble down; he asked why Saul disobeyed the voice of the Lord, and Saul justified himself again. Two admonitions were given and refused before this rejection.

As Samuel turned about to go away, Saul laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent. And Samuel said, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. Just as Saul tore the hem of the garment, so the Lord tore the throne from him; and Samuel says this still before he has ever met David, the same word he gave in chapter 13. And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent. The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan; if a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.

Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel. This spirit is very real: okay, you are right, but do not let the people see the demotion; make sure they still know I am the king. That is the spirit of vanity, caught up in a rank and a title while forgetting that the title came for pleasing the Lord; once you discontinue pleasing the Lord, the title is going to leave as well. So Samuel turned again after Saul, and Saul worshipped the Lord.

Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately, and said, Surely the bitterness of death is past; with Saul under rebuke, Agag figured nobody was mad at the Amalekites anymore and he was safe. And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The old prophet did not play; he finished the commandment himself, measure for measure for what Amalek's sword had done.

Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah, and Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord repented that he had made Saul king over Israel. The mourning is what makes it sad: Samuel raised Saul up from nothing, saw his potential, and saw the Spirit come upon him in chapter 11 when he stood up as a savior for the people; he had hope in him, and it came to this. Samuel was grieved, and the Lord repented of the appointment. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

What Saul was doing when he went to the woman with the familiar spirit is called necromancy. Look that word up: it is when you go to somebody that conjures up spirits. Saul turned to this because the Lord was departed from him and answered him no more, neither by prophets nor by dreams, so he had Samuel conjured up to tell him what to do.

Samuel asks Saul why he inquires of him, seeing the Lord is departed from him and is become his enemy. The Lord did to Saul exactly as he spake by Samuel: he rent the kingdom out of Saul's hand and gave it to his neighbour, even to David. The reason is stated plainly: because Saul obeyed not the voice of the Lord, nor executed his fierce wrath upon Amalek. The Most High gave a law concerning Amalek, and Saul did not carry it out; that history was read earlier in this book.

Tomorrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me means tomorrow you and your sons are going to die; you are going to be with me. Samuel prophesied from his grave, and he also declared that the Lord would deliver the host of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.

Saul fell straightway all along the earth, sore afraid because of the words of Samuel, and there was no strength in him, for he had eaten no bread all the day nor all the night. The woman reminded Saul that she had put her life in her hand and obeyed his voice, and asked him to let her set a morsel of bread before him that he might have strength for his way. He refused at first, but his servants together with the woman compelled him; she killed the fat calf, baked unleavened bread, and they did eat and went away that night. The chapter in sum: Saul inquired of the Lord and was not answered, so he turned to a woman with a familiar spirit and conjured up Samuel. Samuel told him that because of his disobedience the Lord was not dealing with him anymore, and prophesied that tomorrow Saul and his sons would be with him.

Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. The Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons, and slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul's sons. The battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him, and he was sore wounded of the archers.

Saul said unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. What Saul was fearful of is what you see in war, how men will abuse their captives, killing them and abusing their bodies. He was already wounded and could not get away, so instead of being taken captive he told his armourbearer to kill him. His armourbearer would not, for he was sore afraid; therefore Saul took a sword and fell upon it, and when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword and died with him. So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together. Remember what we read in chapter 28: when Saul went and conjured up the spirit of Samuel, Samuel said to him, To morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me. He prophesied unto Saul what was going to happen, and now we read the fulfillment of that prophecy.

When the men of Israel that were on the other side of the valley, and they that were on the other side of Jordan, saw that the men of Israel fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they forsook the cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

On the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen in mount Gilboa. They cut off his head and stripped off his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to publish it in the house of their idols and among the people. They put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan.

When the inhabitants of Jabeshgilead heard of that which the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Bethshan, and came to Jabesh and burnt them there. They took their bones and buried them under a tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days. So in chapter 31 we read of Saul and his sons and his armourbearer dying at the hands of the Philistines. This concludes the history of Saul coming to an end; the second book of Samuel takes up the rise and much of the history concerning King David. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The Philistines fought Israel, the men of Israel fled and fell slain in mount Gilboa, and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul. The battle went hard against Saul, the archers wounded him, and he asked his armourbearer to run him through so the uncircumcised would not abuse him. The armourbearer was too afraid, so Saul fell on his own sword and died. Saul died, his three sons, and all his house together, and when Israel saw it they forsook their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

The next day the Philistines came to strip the slain, found Saul and his sons fallen in Gilboa, took his head and his armour, and sent word throughout their land to carry tidings to their idols and to the people. They put his armour in the house of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon. Dagon was the fish god, and its likeness is carried over into false religion in the fish-shaped mitre and the fish symbol.

When Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all their valiant men arose, took the bodies of Saul and his sons, brought them to Jabesh, buried their bones under the oak, and fasted seven days. It has always been in Israel to mourn our dead. No matter what a person has done, it does not sit right with us to see our brothers put to death. This is why we pray for all Israel to recover themselves.

Saul died for his transgression against the Most High, for not keeping His word, and for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit rather than inquiring of the Most High. Therefore the Most High slew him and turned the kingdom to David the son of Jesse. Saul had gone to a woman with a familiar spirit to bring up Samuel. The left hand of the Most High is real. People who meddle with that get entangled and get spirits put on them. It is not our custom. The last straw for Saul was seeking that familiar spirit. Through Samuel the Most High told him he would join him the next day. The difference is that Samuel died righteously. -

verses.text: And he tarried seven days, according to the set time that Samuel had appointed: but Samuel came not to Gilgal; and the people were scattered from him.
And Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and peace offerings. And he offered the burnt offering.
And it came to pass, that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came; and Saul went out to meet him, that he might salute him.

And Samuel said, What hast thou done? And Saul said, Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash;
Therefore said I, The Philistines will come down now upon me to Gilgal, and I have not made supplication unto the Lord: I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering.

And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever.

But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the Lord commanded thee.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.

But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.

Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at En–dor.

Then said Saul unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. Therefore Saul took a sword, and fell upon it.
And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword, and died with him.
So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together.

So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the Lord, even against the word of the Lord, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it;
And enquired not of the Lord: therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse.
And before his long sleep he made protestations in the sight of the Lord and his anointed, I have not taken any man’s goods, so much as a shoe: and no man did accuse him.
And after his death he prophesied, and shewed the king his end, and lifted up his voice from the earth in prophecy, to blot out the wickedness of the people.
